It involves integrating the model into a new or existing operational change workflow. This could range from executing the model on an ad hoc basis for operational support, integrating real-time predictions of chemical kinetics into an FB or FF control loop, or alerting maintenance teams about potential equipment failures. This stage requires a deep understanding of the operational technology onsite, from SCADA systems to process control algorithms. Deployment takes on many forms, depending on the problem statement and the operational structure of the WRRF. If the objective is autonomous control with a ML prediction (frequently referred to as a digital twin), deployment should be divided into three phases: a digital shadow, supervised control, and unsupervised control. For purposes of this report, a digital shadow is defined as a model that operates in real-time to make predictions but does not actively interact Integration of Data Driven Process Control for Maximizing Energy and Resource Efficiency in WRRFs 23 with controls. The goal of this stage is to observe model behavior “in the wild”; to identify and address unexpected model behavior and quantify performance. The subsequent stages involve allowing the model predictions to be used in control in a setting with and without an additional human-in-the-loop (where a human is directly supervising to ensure the underlying control sequence responds to the new predictions appropriately), respectively. The performance metrics defined during the problem formulation stage should be measured during each phase to ensure that the project merits continuation or needs to be revised. 24 The Water Research Foundation CHAPTER 4 Python Primer for AI in WRRFs 4.1 Introduction to Python For this DOE project, the project team chose Python as the main implementation programming language for the ML Toolkit. Python is a versatile, open-source, high-level programming language known for its simplicity and readability. It has become the go-to language for many fields that are entering the realm of artificial intelligence where Python is heavily used, and recent experiences by team members indicate that Python is quickly becoming the programming language of choice among coders in the water industry. It has extensive libraries, a supportive community, and an ability to easily ingest, analyze, and create models for large amounts of data. For designers and operators of WRRFs who may not have an extensive coding background, Python has a low barrier to entry and a bevy of resources for tutorials and troubleshooting. It can also be easily integrated to run locally on onsite servers or cloud-based platforms. Importantly, popular process modeling platforms (e.g., SUMO, Biowin, GPS-X) have made it possible to seamlessly integrate between their platform and Python. This summary provides an overview of Python, its popularity, essential tools and libraries, and guidance on getting started with Python for AI applications in WRRF systems. 4.1.1 Why Python?
